Apart from its mass and width, the most important property of a new charged gauge boson, $W'$, is the helicity of its couplings to the SM fermions. Such particles are expected to exist in many extensions of the Standard Model. In this paper we explore the capability of the LHC to determine the $W'$ coupling helicity at low integrated luminosities in the $\ell +E_T^{miss}$ discovery channel. We find that measurements of the transverse mass distribution, reconstructed from this final state in the $W-W'$ interference region, provides the best determination of this quantity. To make such measurements requires integrated luminosities of $\sim 10(60) fb^{-1}$ assuming $M_{W'}=1.5(2.5)$ TeV and provided that the $W'$ couplings have Standard Model magnitude. This helicity determination can be further strengthened by the use of various discovery channel leptonic asymmetries, also measured in the same interference regime, but with higher integrated luminosities.

# Determining the Coupling Helicity of a New Charged Gauge Boson at the LHC

Beyond its mass and width, the most important property characterizing a new charged gauge boson (W′) is the helicity of its couplings to Standard Model fermions. This helicity structure encodes fundamental information about the nature of the underlying physics giving rise to the W′, distinguishing between different theoretical scenarios and revealing whether the new boson couples preferentially to left- or right-handed fermions. Consequently, establishing the coupling helicity is essential for interpreting any discovery of such a particle and understanding its place within extensions of the Standard Model.

This paper investigates the ability of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) to determine the W′ coupling helicity at low integrated luminosities. Our analysis focuses on the ℓ + missing transverse energy discovery channel, which represents the primary and most sensitive avenue for the initial observation of a new charged gauge boson at hadron colliders. By concentrating on this channel, we assess how quickly, following a discovery, the helicity of the W′ couplings can be established.

We find that measurements of the transverse mass distribution in the region where the W and W′ amplitudes interfere provide the most effective means of determining the coupling helicity. The interference between the Standard Model W boson and the new W′ boson is sensitive to the relative helicity structure of their couplings, and the resulting modifications to the transverse mass spectrum offer a clear observable signature that discriminates between the different helicity hypotheses.

Quantitatively, these measurements require integrated luminosities of approximately 10 fb⁻¹ for a W′ mass of 1.5 TeV, rising to about 60 fb⁻¹ for a mass of 2.5 TeV, assuming coupling magnitudes equal to those of the Standard Model. These modest luminosity requirements indicate that a determination of the coupling helicity is feasible relatively early in the LHC program, particularly for lighter W′ masses.

Finally, the helicity determination can be further strengthened by exploiting various leptonic asymmetries measured within the same interference regime. These asymmetries provide complementary information that reinforces the conclusions drawn from the transverse mass distribution. However, because such asymmetry measurements are statistically more demanding, they require correspondingly higher integrated luminosities to achieve comparable significance.

# Determining W′ Coupling Helicity at the LHC

## Introduction

The search for physics beyond the Standard Model (SM) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) encompasses a broad range of hypothetical particles predicted by numerous theoretical frameworks. Among these, additional charged gauge bosons, generically denoted W′, feature prominently in extensions of the SM gauge structure. Such particles arise naturally in models incorporating extended gauge symmetries, including left-right symmetric models, grand unified theories, and various scenarios of extra spatial dimensions. Should a W′ boson be discovered, a crucial next step will be to characterize its properties—most importantly, the nature of its couplings to SM fermions. In particular, determining whether the W′ couples with left-handed, right-handed, or mixed chirality provides a powerful discriminator between competing theoretical models.

This paper investigates the LHC's ability to determine the coupling helicity of a new charged gauge boson to Standard Model fermions at relatively low integrated luminosities. We focus on the most accessible discovery channel, in which the W′ decays into a charged lepton and a neutrino, yielding an experimental signature of a single high-transverse-momentum lepton accompanied by significant missing transverse energy (ℓ + missing transverse energy).

## Methodology and Analysis

The central challenge in helicity determination stems from the fact that the neutrino escapes detection, precluding full reconstruction of the decay kinematics in the leptonic channel. Consequently, one must rely on observables constructed from measurable quantities—principally the transverse mass of the lepton–neutrino system and various angular and asymmetry observables.

Our analysis reveals that the transverse mass distribution offers the most effective handle on the coupling helicity. Crucially, the discriminating power resides not in the resonant peak region itself but in the interference region between the W and W′ contributions. The quantum mechanical interference between the SM W boson and the new W′ boson depends sensitively on the chirality of the W′ couplings: left-handed couplings interfere with the SM amplitude in a manner distinct from right-handed couplings, which may not interfere at all with the purely left-handed SM charged current. This interference imprints a characteristic shape on the transverse mass spectrum below the W′ resonance, providing a clean observable for distinguishing coupling scenarios.

## Results

By exploiting the transverse mass distribution reconstructed in the W–W′ interference region, we find that the LHC can achieve a meaningful determination of the W′ coupling helicity with modest data samples. Specifically, our analysis indicates that an integrated luminosity of approximately 10 fb⁻¹ suffices to establish the coupling helicity for a W′ boson with a mass of 1.5 TeV. For a heavier W′ with a mass of 2.5 TeV, the reduced production cross section necessitates a correspondingly larger data sample of approximately 60 fb⁻¹ to reach comparable sensitivity. These luminosity requirements are well within the reach of the LHC operating at design energy, demonstrating that helicity determination can be accomplished relatively early in the experimental program following a discovery.

The sensitivity obtained from the transverse mass analysis can be further enhanced by incorporating leptonic asymmetry measurements. The forward-backward and charge asymmetries of the final-state lepton carry additional information about the chiral structure of the W′ couplings, since the angular distribution of the decay products reflects the polarization state dictated by the coupling helicity. Combining these asymmetry observables with the transverse mass information strengthens the overall discrimination between left-handed and right-handed coupling hypotheses, improving the statistical significance and potentially reducing the required integrated luminosity.

## Conclusion

In summary, we have demonstrated that the LHC possesses the capability to determine the coupling helicity of a newly discovered W′ boson using the leptonic discovery channel at accessible integrated luminosities. The transverse mass distribution in the W–W′ interference region emerges as the primary discriminating observable, requiring roughly 10 (60) fb⁻¹ for a 1.5 (2.5) TeV W′, with additional improvement available through leptonic asymmetry measurements. These findings underscore that, beyond mere discovery, the LHC can provide valuable insight into the underlying theoretical structure responsible for an extended electroweak gauge sector, thereby helping to identify the specific model realized in nature.

# Setting Yourself Apart Through Standards

In a world where competition grows fiercer by the day, standing **apart** from the crowd is more important than ever. Whether in business, academics, or personal development, the ability to distinguish yourself often comes down to the standards you set and the consistency with which you uphold them.

## The Power of High Standards

**Standard** practices exist for a reason—they provide a baseline of quality and reliability. However, meeting the minimum requirement rarely leads to exceptional results. Those who truly excel understand that a **standard** is not a finish line but a starting point. They ask themselves how they can exceed expectations rather than simply satisfy them.

Consider two employees performing the same task. One completes the work to the acceptable **standard**, while the other adds thoughtful attention to detail, anticipates future problems, and delivers something extraordinary. The difference between them is not talent alone—it is a mindset that refuses to settle.

## What Sets People Apart

**Such** qualities as discipline, curiosity, and integrity are what genuinely separate high achievers from everyone else. **Such** traits cannot be faked; they reveal themselves over time through consistent action. When you commit to habits like these, you naturally set yourself **apart** from those who rely on shortcuts or momentary bursts of effort.

Interestingly, the qualities that set us **apart** are rarely dramatic. They are often small, repeated choices—arriving prepared, following through on promises, and holding yourself accountable when no one is watching.

## Conclusion

**Apart** from raw ability, it is our **standards** and daily habits that shape our success. By embracing **such** principles and refusing to accept mediocrity, anyone can rise above the ordinary and create a lasting impact. The choice, ultimately, belongs to you.

# Abstract

We present a comprehensive analysis of methods for determining the coupling helicity of a hypothetical W′ gauge boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Many extensions of the Standard Model, including left-right symmetric models, non-universal gauge theories, and certain grand unified frameworks, predict additional charged vector bosons whose chiral coupling structure encodes essential information about the underlying symmetry-breaking mechanism. We demonstrate that the helicity of the W′ coupling to Standard Model fermions can be extracted through the angular distributions of decay products in the process pp → W′ → ℓν, exploiting the correlation between the boson polarization and the charged lepton emission angle. Using a full detector-level simulation at √s = 14 TeV, we show that the forward-backward asymmetry and the transverse mass distribution provide complementary discriminating observables sensitive to purely left-handed, purely right-handed, and mixed coupling scenarios. We quantify the integrated luminosity required to distinguish these hypotheses at the 3σ and 5σ confidence levels as a function of the W′ mass, accounting for dominant backgrounds and systematic uncertainties from parton distribution functions and detector resolution. Our results indicate that for a W′ with mass up to 4 TeV, the coupling chirality can be robustly determined with 300 fb⁻¹ of data, offering a powerful diagnostic tool for identifying the theoretical origin of any newly discovered charged gauge boson.

# Determination of W′ Coupling Helicity at the LHC with Low Integrated Luminosity

## Abstract

We investigate the capability of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) to discriminate between left-handed and right-handed couplings of a hypothetical charged gauge boson W′ at early stages of operation, corresponding to low integrated luminosities. Many extensions of the Standard Model—including left-right symmetric models, Kaluza-Klein excitations, and Little Higgs scenarios—predict additional heavy charged gauge bosons whose chiral structure encodes essential information about the underlying symmetry-breaking mechanism. We perform a detailed analysis of the process pp → W′ → ℓν, focusing on the leptonic decay channel to muons and electrons. 

While the transverse mass distribution of the charged lepton–missing energy system provides a robust means of establishing the W′ mass and production cross section, we demonstrate that this observable alone is largely insensitive to the coupling helicity. To resolve this ambiguity, we exploit the parity-violating nature of the couplings through measurements of the charge asymmetry and the forward-backward asymmetry of the decay lepton. These leptonic asymmetries exhibit a characteristic dependence on the chiral structure, arising from the interference between the valence quark parton distributions and the angular distribution of the decay products.

Using a fast detector simulation, we quantify the statistical significance with which the left- and right-handed hypotheses can be distinguished as a function of the W′ mass and integrated luminosity. Our results indicate that for W′ masses up to approximately 2 TeV, the coupling helicity can be determined at the 3σ level with integrated luminosities as low as 1–10 fb⁻¹ at √s = 14 TeV. We discuss the dependence of these conclusions on parton distribution function uncertainties and detector acceptance effects, and comment on the complementarity of asymmetry-based observables with rate measurements for early new-physics characterization at the LHC.

---

*Keywords:* W′ boson, coupling helicity, transverse mass, leptonic asymmetry, forward-backward asymmetry, LHC, beyond the Standard Model

# Abstract

We investigate the prospects for determining the chiral coupling structure of a new charged gauge boson (W′) at the Large Hadron Collider. While the discovery of a W′ resonance in the transverse mass spectrum of the leptonic decay channel provides limited information on its underlying dynamics, the angular distribution of the decay leptons offers a powerful discriminator between purely left-handed and right-handed couplings. We construct forward-backward and center-edge asymmetry observables that are sensitive to the interference between W′ exchange and Standard Model backgrounds, as well as to the polarization of the produced gauge boson. Performing a detailed analysis including realistic detector acceptance and parton distribution uncertainties, we find that distinguishing left- from right-handed couplings at the 95% confidence level requires approximately 30 fb⁻¹ of integrated luminosity for a W′ mass of 1.5 TeV, increasing to roughly 100 fb⁻¹ for a mass of 2.5 TeV. These results demonstrate that chirality determination is feasible during standard LHC operation.
